project.title: SGEMM GPU Kernel Performance - Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
project.description: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) implementation from scratch (Random With Replacement vs. Random Without Replacement) on the SGEMM GPU Kernel Performance dataset across various batch sizes.
project.author: Santanu Samanta

dataset.name: SGEMM GPU Kernel Performance Dataset
dataset.target: Log-transformed and averaged execution time (Run1 to Run4 in ms)

strategies.name: Random With Replacement
strategies.description: Batches are sampled randomly with replacement during each epoch iteration.

strategies.name: Random Without Replacement
strategies.description: Data indices are shuffled randomly at the start of each epoch and traversed sequentially without replacement.

notebook_cells.title: Imports & Environment Initialization
notebook_cells.source:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

np.random.seed(42) # for future reproducibility
notebook_cells.intuition: Initializes the foundational numerical computing packages (`numpy` for vectorized tensor operations and `pandas` for tabular data structures). Locking the pseudorandom number generator seed (np.random.seed(42)) ensures that random sampling and weight initialization remain strictly deterministic and reproducible across training runs.

notebook_cells.title: Dataset & Feature Overview
notebook_cells.source: Info about features and dataset structure.
notebook_cells.intuition: Documents the high-dimensional feature space of the SGEMM benchmark. Each instance represents a distinct GPU kernel configuration combining tiling parameters, work-group dimensions, and unrolling factors.

notebook_cells.title: Dataset Loading & Structural Inspection
notebook_cells.source:
df = pd.read_csv("sgemm_product.csv")
print(f"Dataset shape:{df.shape}")
df.info()
print(df.describe())
print(df.head())
notebook_cells.intuition: Loads the 241,600 rows into memory and performs exploratory data analysis (EDA). We inspect data types, memory footprint (33.2 MB), and descriptive statistics to check for scale disparities across the 14 integer tuning features and 4 float execution runs.

notebook_cells.title: Feature Extraction Phase
notebook_cells.source: Separating features (first 14 columns) and target (last 4 execution runs).
notebook_cells.intuition: Separates independent input variables (X) representing GPU kernel compile options from the dependent output benchmarks (Runs 1 to 4 in milliseconds).

notebook_cells.title: Feature Matrix & Target Extraction
notebook_cells.intuition: Slices the pandas DataFrame into pure NumPy ndarrays. X holds shape (241600, 14) and runs holds shape (241600, 4), preparing raw data for vectorized linear algebra computations.

notebook_cells.title: Target Transformation & Log-Averaging
notebook_cells.source: Taking the log average of run columns to stabilize variance and simplify calculations.
notebook_cells.intuition: GPU execution times span multiple orders of magnitude (from 13ms to 3300ms), causing severe heteroscedasticity. Taking the arithmetic mean across the 4 runs followed by the natural logarithm compresses the dynamic range into a stable normal-like distribution.

notebook_cells.title: Target Vector Construction
notebook_cells.intuition: Computes the target vector Y through equation: Y = ln((Run1 + Run2 + Run3 + Run4) / 4). This logarithmic compression stabilizes gradient updates and prevents extreme execution outliers from destabilizing the cost function.

notebook_cells.title: Mathematical Formulation of Loss & Gradients
notebook_cells.source: Defining core mathematical functions: MSE Loss, Gradient wrt Weights, and Gradient wrt Bias.
notebook_cells.intuition: Establishes the convex optimization foundation. Linear regression predicts execution time via dot product: y_pred = X dot W + b. The Mean Squared Error (MSE) measures aggregate squared residuals.

notebook_cells.title: Loss Function & Partial Derivative Implementation
notebook_cells.intuition: Implements exact calculus formulas. Loss function: L = (1 / 2n) * sum((X dot W + b - Y)^2). Weight gradient: dL/dW = (1/n) * X^T * (y_pred - Y). Bias gradient: dL/db = (1/n) * sum(y_pred - Y). Division by 2 simplifies the power rule derivative nicely.

notebook_cells.title: Strategy 1: Random With Replacement (RWR)
notebook_cells.source: Strategy 1: Random With Replacement sampling per epoch iteration.
notebook_cells.intuition: In RWR, mini-batches are drawn uniformly at random with replacement. This models independent Poisson sampling where identical rows can be sampled multiple times within the same epoch update cycle.

notebook_cells.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent With Replacement
notebook_cells.source:
def sgd_RWR(X,Y,alpha=0.01,epochs=100,batch_size=240, bias=0):
    m, n = X.shape
    w = np.zeros(n)
    itt_per_epoch = int(np.ceil(m/batch_size))
    loss_plot = []
    for i in range(epochs):
        for j in range(itt_per_epoch):
            indexes = np.random.choice(m, size=batch_size, replace=True)
            w -= alpha * gradw(X[indexes], Y[indexes], w, bias)
            bias -= alpha * gradb(X[indexes], Y[indexes], w, bias)
        loss_plot.append(MSE(X, Y, w, bias))
    return w, bias, loss_plot
notebook_cells.intuition: Performs stochastic updates: W_new = W_old - alpha * dL/dW using randomly bootstrapped batch indices generated via `np.random.choice(m, size=batch_size, replace=True)`.

notebook_cells.title: Strategy 2: Random Without Replacement (RWOR)
notebook_cells.source: Strategy 2: Random Without Replacement via epoch permutation.
notebook_cells.intuition: RWOR shuffles dataset row indices at the start of every epoch and slices sequential non-overlapping chunks. This guarantees every single instance is visited exactly once per epoch, reducing estimator variance.

notebook_cells.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent Without Replacement
notebook_cells.source:
def sgd_RWOR(X,Y,alpha=0.01,epochs=100,batch_size=240,bias=0):
    m, n = X.shape
    w = np.zeros(n)
    loss_plot = []
    for i in range(epochs):
        indexes = np.random.permutation(m)
        X_p, Y_p = X[indexes], Y[indexes]
        for j in range(0, m, batch_size):
            w -= alpha * gradw(X_p[j:j+batch_size], Y_p[j:j+batch_size], w, bias)
            bias -= alpha * gradb(X_p[j:j+batch_size], Y_p[j:j+batch_size], w, bias)
        loss_plot.append(MSE(X, Y, w, bias))
    return w, bias, loss_plot
notebook_cells.intuition: Utilizes `np.random.permutation(m)` to permute indices once per epoch. Batches of size `batch_size` traverse through the permuted dataset sequentially without duplication.

notebook_cells.title: Data Splitting & Z-Score Standardization
notebook_cells.source: Train-test data splitting (80/20) and feature standardization (z-score normalization).
notebook_cells.intuition: Performs an 80-20 train-test split and applies Z-score normalization: X_scaled = (X - mu) / sigma. Feature scaling is mathematically vital so that gradient descent converges uniformly across features with vastly different physical units.

notebook_cells.title: Train-Test Split & Standardization Pipeline
notebook_cells.source:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_train, X_test, Y_train, Y_test = train_test_split(X, Y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
mu, sigma = X_train.mean(axis=0), X_train.std(axis=0)
X_train = (X_train - mu) / sigma
X_test = (X_test - mu) / sigma
notebook_cells.intuition: Computes mean (mu) and standard deviation (sigma) exclusively on the training partition to prevent data leakage, subsequently standardizing both train and test matrices.

notebook_cells.title: Strategy 1 Training & Evaluation
notebook_cells.source:
Epochs = 100
Alpha = 0.00050
batch_sizes = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]
for bs in batch_sizes:
    w_1, bias1, yy1 = sgd_RWR(X_train, Y_train, alpha=Alpha, epochs=Epochs, batch_size=bs)
test_mse_1 = MSE(X_test, Y_test, w_1, bias1)
print(f"Final Test MSE Strategy 1: {test_mse_1:.4f}")
notebook_cells.intuition: Trains the model using Strategy 1 across multiple batch sizes over 100 epochs, evaluating generalization performance on unseen test data.
notebook_cells.output: Final Test MSE using Weight Vector from Strategy 1: 0.2790

notebook_cells.title: Strategy 2 Training & Evaluation
notebook_cells.source:
for bs in batch_sizes:
    w_2, bias2, yy2 = sgd_RWOR(X_train, Y_train, alpha=Alpha, epochs=Epochs, batch_size=bs)
test_mse_2 = MSE(X_test, Y_test, w_2, bias2)
print(f"Final Test MSE Strategy 2: {test_mse_2:.4f}")
notebook_cells.intuition: Trains the model using Strategy 2 across identical batch sizes, confirming robust convergence with a final test MSE of 0.2790.
notebook_cells.output: Final Test MSE using Weight Vector from Strategy 2: 0.2790
